checkpoints: Kafka's default partitioner hashes the message key to select a partition, so every event sharing the same key value always lands on the same partition, no matter how much total traffic the topic sees.

A partition key with low cardinality — such as `countryCode`, which only has around 15 distinct values — concentrates most events onto whichever partition the dominant value hashes to when real-world traffic is skewed toward one value, collapsing effective parallelism down to that single partition's consumer.

Kafka assigns at most one consumer per partition within a consumer group, so adding more consumers to an already-provisioned topic cannot reduce lag on one overloaded partition; the bottleneck is structural (key design), not a capacity shortage that more consumers would fix.

The correct fix is to change what the key represents rather than scale out consumers: re-keying on a high-cardinality, evenly-distributed field such as `orderId` or `accountId` spreads events roughly evenly across all partitions instead of piling onto one.

When ordering must genuinely be preserved for the scope currently baked into a low-cardinality key, a composite sub-key such as `countryCode#hashBucket(orderId, N)` keeps FIFO order within each bucket while spreading that key's overall volume across N partitions instead of one.

Sub-key sharding is a trade-off, not a free win: events are only guaranteed to stay in order within their bucket, not across the full original key's traffic, so the narrower ordering guarantee has to be an explicit, conscious choice rather than an assumed side effect.

Most real ordering invariants are per-entity (e.g. per-order or per-account) rather than per-broad-category (e.g. per-country), so re-scoping the partition key to the entity that actually needs ordering is usually both the correct guarantee and the higher-throughput choice.

Diagnosing and validating a hot-partition problem both rely on per-partition lag and offset data — via a tool like `kafka-consumer-groups --describe` or a lag dashboard — checked before and after a key change under comparably skewed load to confirm load actually redistributes evenly rather than just assuming the fix worked.
